stem: A shelf contains 11 fiction books and 7 nonfiction books. If one book is selected at random, what is the probability that it is a nonfiction book?
explanation: There are 11 + 7 = 18 books total, and 7 are nonfiction, so the probability is 7/18. The distractor 11/18 results from selecting the fiction count instead of nonfiction. The distractor 7/11 uses the fiction count as the denominator rather than the total. The distractor 7/25 uses an incorrect total of 25 instead of 18.

stem: A survey of 200 commuters found that 74 take the bus, 53 take the train, and 19 take both the bus and the train. If a commuter from this survey is chosen at random, what is the probability that the commuter takes the bus or the train?
explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: P(bus or train) = (74 + 53 - 19)/200 = 108/200. The distractor 127/200 adds 74 + 53 = 127 without subtracting the 19 who take both, double-counting that group. The distractor 146/200 adds all three values (74 + 53 + 19) instead of subtracting the overlap. The distractor 19/200 gives the probability of taking both rather than either.

stem: At a veterinary clinic, 38% of patients are dogs, 27% are cats, and the rest are other animals. Among dogs, 15% have been diagnosed with a joint condition. Among cats, 9% have been diagnosed with the same joint condition, and among other animals, 4% have. Given that a randomly selected patient has the joint condition, what is the probability that the patient is a dog? (Round to the nearest hundredth.)
explanation: This requires Bayes' theorem. The other animals make up 100% - 38% - 27% = 35%. P(joint condition) = 0.38(0.15) + 0.27(0.09) + 0.35(0.04) = 0.0570 + 0.0243 + 0.0140 = 0.0953. Then P(dog | joint condition) = 0.0570/0.0953 = 0.5981, which rounds to 0.60. The distractor 0.57 comes from dividing 0.0570 by 0.10 (rounding the denominator up) or a similar shortcut error. The distractor 0.15 confuses P(joint condition | dog) with P(dog | joint condition), reversing the conditional. The distractor 0.38 uses the unconditional probability of being a dog without applying Bayes' theorem.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 150 students at a university found that 42% prefer online exams. The margin of error for this estimate is 6 percentage points. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Between 36% and 48% of all students at the university likely prefer online exams.
Exactly 42% of all students at the university prefer online exams.
Between 36% and 48% of the 150 students surveyed prefer online exams.
42% of all universities have students who prefer online exams.

explanation: A margin of error of 6 percentage points around a sample proportion of 42% produces a confidence interval of 36% to 48% for the population parameter. The distractor stating exactly 42% ignores the margin of error, treating the sample statistic as the exact population parameter. The distractor limiting the interval to the 150 surveyed students confuses the sample (already measured) with the population being estimated. The distractor about 42% of universities misidentifies the population entirely.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 400 registered voters and finds that 57% support a local bond measure, with a margin of error of 4.2 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. A second researcher surveys a random sample of 1,600 registered voters from the same population and obtains the same sample proportion. Which of the following best describes how the margin of error for the second survey compares to that of the first?

options.text: The margin of error for the second survey is approximately half that of the first survey.
The margin of error for the second survey is approximately one-fourth that of the first survey.
The margin of error for the second survey is approximately equal to that of the first survey.
The margin of error for the second survey is approximately double that of the first survey.

explanation: The margin of error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size. Since the second sample (1,600) is 4 times the first (400), the margin of error decreases by a factor of the square root of 4, which is 2, making it approximately half the original. The distractor claiming one-fourth incorrectly treats the margin of error as inversely proportional to the sample size itself rather than its square root. The distractor claiming the margins are equal ignores the effect of sample size. The distractor claiming double reverses the relationship between sample size and margin of error.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A polling firm surveys a random sample of 900 residents in a city and finds that 61% favor expanding the public transit system, with a margin of error of 3.2 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. A journalist reports that this result proves at least 55% of all city residents favor the expansion. Which of the following statements best evaluates the journalist's claim?

options.text: The claim is supported because the entire 95% confidence interval (57.8% to 64.2%) is above 55%.
The claim is not supported because the sample proportion could differ from the population proportion.
The claim is supported because 61% is greater than 55%.
The claim is not supported because 55% does not fall within the confidence interval.

explanation: The 95% confidence interval is 61% plus or minus 3.2%, which gives 57.8% to 64.2%. Since the entire interval lies above 55%, there is strong statistical evidence that the true population proportion exceeds 55%, supporting the journalist's claim. The distractor arguing the claim is unsupported merely because sample and population values can differ is too vague and ignores that the confidence interval quantifies that uncertainty. The distractor citing only that 61% is greater than 55% uses the point estimate without accounting for the margin of error, which is incomplete reasoning. The distractor stating the claim fails because 55% is outside the interval misinterprets the logic: the relevant question is whether the interval is entirely above 55%, not whether 55% is inside it.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A health magazine reports that people who eat breakfast daily have, on average, lower body mass index (BMI) than people who skip breakfast. The data came from a survey of 2,400 adults who self-reported their eating habits. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Eating breakfast daily causes a lower BMI.
There is an association between eating breakfast daily and having a lower BMI.
Skipping breakfast causes a higher BMI.
Adults who eat breakfast exercise more than adults who skip breakfast.

explanation: Because the study is observational (a survey with self-reported data and no random assignment to treatment groups), it can only establish an association, not a causal relationship. The distractor claiming breakfast causes lower BMI incorrectly infers causation from an observational study. The distractor claiming skipping breakfast causes higher BMI similarly makes an unsupported causal claim from observational data. The distractor about exercise introduces an unsubstantiated claim not supported by the data described.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: Researchers want to test whether a new ergonomic keyboard reduces wrist pain in office workers. They recruit 130 volunteers from a large corporation and randomly assign 65 to use the new keyboard for 8 weeks and 65 to continue using their standard keyboard. At the end of the study, the group using the new keyboard reports significantly less wrist pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: The new keyboard caused a reduction in wrist pain among the volunteers in the study.
The new keyboard will reduce wrist pain for all office workers.
There is an association between keyboard type and wrist pain, but causation cannot be established.
The reduction in wrist pain was likely due to the placebo effect rather than the keyboard.

explanation: Because the study uses random assignment to treatment and control groups, it is an experiment, which can support a causal conclusion. The causal claim is limited to the volunteers in the study since they were not randomly selected from a broader population. The distractor extending the conclusion to all office workers overgeneralizes beyond the study's volunteers, who were not a random sample of all office workers. The distractor denying causation applies the rule for observational studies, but this is an experiment with random assignment, which does support causal claims. The distractor attributing results to placebo effect is speculation not supported by the study design described.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A school district randomly selects 300 eighth-graders from all eighth-graders in the district and randomly assigns them to two groups: one group uses a new math tutoring app for one semester, and the other group receives no additional resources. At the end of the semester, the group using the app scores significantly higher on a standardized math test. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.text: The tutoring app caused higher test scores, but only for the students in the study.
The tutoring app caused higher test scores, and this result can be generalized to all eighth-graders in the district.
There is an association between using the app and higher scores, but no causal conclusion can be drawn.
The tutoring app will improve test scores for eighth-graders in any school district.

explanation: The study uses both random selection (from all eighth-graders in the district) and random assignment (to treatment and control groups). Random assignment supports a causal conclusion, and random selection supports generalizing to the population from which the sample was drawn, which is all eighth-graders in the district. The distractor limiting the conclusion to only the study participants ignores that random selection from the district population allows generalization to that population. The distractor denying any causal conclusion incorrectly applies the observational-study limitation to a randomized experiment. The distractor extending to any school district overgeneralizes beyond the population from which the random sample was drawn.
